# Negotiation Cache and Queue Creation Troubleshooting Guide

The initial symptom is that, during a transport compatibility check, negotiation probe state appears to have carried over from the previous attempt, or a connection pool queue is already present unexpectedly. First record these as two separate observations; they may occur together, but that alone does not establish a common cause.

**Check the negotiation probe first.** If all you can establish from the incident is "this time was different from last time," with no clues as to whether the same transport object was reused between the two probes, stop here. Record the known negotiation results, whether another probe was initiated, and whether the state was observed before or after the probe. Don't replace these facts with "the cache wasn't cleared."

If state still carries over on a path known to create a new object, keep a record of that path and where the state was observed; next, check only how probe state is saved and read. If state does not carry over but the results are still inconsistent, label this branch "probe state not reproduced" and move on to the connection pool side. Don't keep speculating about the cache.

**Then check the queue.** First distinguish whether the queue was visible before a connection was obtained or only after a transport operation. The former only shows that the current entry point already holds a queue object; in the latter case, record the action that triggered it separately. Don't combine success and failure into one conclusion: if queue appearance timing differs between the two paths, record each separately. Don't infer what happens on the other path from a single result.

If there is no evidence of connection returns, waiting, or reuse after the queue appears, do not write it up as pool exhaustion. Stop expanding the investigation here; first complete the record of the triggering action and its order relative to the queue's appearance. If queue creation timing is consistent but request results still vary with negotiation state, return to the previous branch and prioritize checking whether probe state is being read.

**Code starting point.** Start with `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` and inspect the setup and close paths around the transport object. Dependencies visible in the file include `io`, `socket`, and `ssl`; as you read, annotate socket-layer actions separately from TLS-layer actions to avoid mistaking local behavior of the SSL transport wrapper for connection pool policy. Start by checking the objects near the observed symptoms; don't infer where negotiation caching or queues are implemented from path names.

At a minimum, record three things in the investigation notes: whether what appeared was negotiation state or a queue object; where it was observed in relation to the action, before or after; and whether the result can be reproduced through the same entry point. If any of the three is missing, write the conclusion as "unconfirmed." Only assess whether they are related once state carryover and queue creation order have each been recorded.

If you reach a branch you cannot pin down, just retain the object names from that point and where you stopped. Don't add explanations for cache invalidation, queue warmup, or connection reuse just to complete the record; those claims need supporting references from follow-up work.

# HTTP/2 chunked header migration notes

This record is kept near the old transport compatibility wrap-up.`test/with_dummyserver/test_chunked_transfer.py` was once the easiest inspection entry point: the filename and scenario both pointed to chunked transport, and nearby there were socket, pytest and the dummyserver test base class. It remains referenced, not because all HTTP/2 behavior has already been explained here, but because the migration work at the time did in fact start from this server-side fixture.

The draft reduced the issue to one sentence: It is enough for HTTP/2 to no longer carry a chunked header. This is the old wording and cannot be used directly as the completion criterion. It conflated the protocol path, request construction, and server-side reception into one layer, and also assumed that every relevant request would land in the same test block. The old chunked test case originally addressed the chunked-transfer scenario; the HTTP/2 check merely borrowed the existing request entry point and server observation points from it. The fixture can be reused, but the assertions should not therefore be merged.

At the time, the old scenario was not deleted. The reason for keeping it was practical: during troubleshooting, it was necessary to first distinguish whether the original chunked request had changed or the newly added HTTP/2 call had not reached the server as expected. If the two cases left only one failure output, readers could easily change the HTTP/1 assertion first, yet ultimately fail to answer what the HTTP/2 request looked like after passing through transport.

```text
Old path
chunked request ──> dummyserver scenario ──> existing assertions

Separated verification after migration
HTTP/1 request ──> retain the chunked scenario
HTTP/2 request ──> independent call ──> dummyserver receive record
```

This diagram shows the troubleshooting order used at the time, not a call relationship diagram. It only requires first identifying which path the request being examined belongs to, then returning to the server-side record; a single HTTP/1 failure cannot directly establish the header handling of HTTP/2. The test filename containing chunked only indicates that it retains the relevant scenario; it does not mean that all HTTP/2 requests are assembled here.

## What was retained when moving out of the old scenario

The first migration step was not to change the expected header set, but to confirm that the old scenario could still run and make its judgment independently. The request construction, server reception point, and original assertion location were left in place. That way, adjusting the HTTP/2 check would not incidentally rewrite the chunked transfer itself. Even if the old assertion only answers whether the chunked request succeeded, it should continue to answer only that question.

Next, use a minimal scenario skeleton to provide an entry point for the HTTP/2 call. What is copied is the server-side observation setup, not the old protocol's assertion text. It is not enough to add the protocol name beside an existing call, nor can you first remove `Transfer-Encoding` from the expectation and then claim that migration is complete; if the call in fact still takes the old path, the absence of the header field cannot show that HTTP/2 has been checked.

On the server side, record whether the request arrived, along with the headers visible to the receiving end and the request result. This does not require turning every header into a whitelist. The old record is concerned with whether a request using HTTP/2 still carries the old chunked representation. The client-side object pending transmission is insufficient to answer this question: it only shows what the caller prepared, not what the transport layer ultimately handed to the server.

The investigation under RHC-214 kept one successful call and one failed call as separate records. This split is more useful during migration than "pass or fail". A successful call should be associated with the server's receive record; for a failed call, first determine whether it stopped before sending, during transport, or after server reception. If the request never reached dummyserver at all, do not lump it together with a post-reception header difference as one sample. Early records included wording that directly called an assertion failure a failed call; that wording is no longer suitable for continued use.

## The operation order used at the time

1. First confirm that the server observation point for the original chunked scenario is still present; do not start by changing the request parameters.
2. Provide an independent entry point for the HTTP/2 call, avoiding putting the protocol branch into the old assertion.
3. First check whether the successful call left a request result on the dummyserver side; if there is no result, keep the investigation at the level of whether the call entered the target transport path.
4. Then record the stop position of the failed call. Failures before arrival and failures after reception are saved separately; neither replaces the other.
5. Only when the HTTP/2 request has been seen by the server should you check whether the old chunked representation still appears.
6. Run the original chunked scenario and the HTTP/2 scenario separately. Only after the two results can each explain its own object should they be retained as migration records that can be revisited.

This order has one more step than "change the header fields and then run the tests", but it avoids the most common misreading on the old page: treating the test path as the location where the transport is implemented. The socket dependency here was also once mistakenly taken to be a part that the HTTP/2 scenario had to retain. That was only an old inference drawn from direct adjacency in the file, not a requirement of the transport interface; whether a specific scenario still needs it should be decided by the scenario itself.

## Practices that are no longer suitable to copy

The old draft suggested that, as long as the result of HTTP/2 did not show `Transfer-Encoding`, the compatibility check could end. This suggestion is kept here as historical context, but it is no longer sufficient. Before treating the field as absent, first confirm that the request actually took the path under review; at the same time, determine whether the failed call reached the server at all. Without these two pieces of information, "no such header" may simply mean that the wrong object was inspected.

Another old practice was to change the old assertion first and then add the server-side record. That can produce a superficially clean test result, but it cannot distinguish whether the comparison is against the pre-send object or the request after reception. During migration, obtain the server-side record first, then make the assertion converge on the corresponding path. The original chunked test case does not need to take on the final determination of HTTP/2 for this purpose.

Nor is it recommended to use a conditional branch to push the two paths back into a single expectation. If the server has already seen the HTTP/2 request and it differs from the old assumption, the difference itself should remain in an independent scenario. Whether to extract a shared helper or adjust the ownership of a higher-level interface is not determined by this old migration record.

## Restoring the old path

When a newly added HTTP/2 scenario affects the original chunked test case, the restoration should be small: remove the new scenario's changes to the old assertion, retain the original chunked request and the original server observation point; keep the HTTP/2 call and its receive record in an independent test for continued investigation. Restoring the old path does not mean that HTTP/2 has been confirmed; it only means that the original scenario is once again judging only the original object.

If the failed call never reaches dummyserver, do not temporarily add more header assertions to the old chunked test case as a workaround. Keep the sample as a pre-arrival failure, retain the call entry point, and trace back the transport or negotiation point. At this point, the old test continues to check chunked behavior and cannot be used as a substitute for the result of HTTP/2.

If the request has already reached the server but the record is inconsistent with the old assumption, give priority to preserving the original receive record and the independent assertion. Do not erase the difference just to make the two paths share one expectation. Only after the actual interface ownership is clear should you decide whether a shared helper is needed.

## Later marginal notes

In later follow-up, RHC-214 still left "HTTP/2 chunked Header Suppression" as an unconfirmed item. Here, unconfirmed means that this old check did not fill in the final server-side sample and is insufficient to infer reverse behavior. The card only provides an investigation entry point; follow-up checking still starts with the scenario in the chunked test file.

DOC-24 preserves an adjacent HTTP/2 entry-point experiment. The two pages can be found together, but the record for NPN Query Entry Point Removal cannot replace the request-header check here: the former concerns the negotiation entry point, while the latter concerns the content presented by the request at the server after it passes through transport.

Only three items have not yet been added to this page: the location of the server-side record for the target HTTP/2 call, which segment the failed call belongs to, and whether the old chunked scenario can still explain its own result independently.

# ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility Record

This record began with a small issue while wrapping up transport compatibility: the value of ALPN not only needs to be passed to the TLS layer, but must also retain a collection shape that existing callers recognize. The initial investigation started with `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py`. The file header shows `from __future__ import annotations` and three direct dependencies, `io`, `socket`, and `ssl`, making it a reasonable place to start reading; these adjacency relationships alone are not enough to prove that the collection shape is constructed or ultimately determined here.

The working hypothesis at the time was that this was more likely a representation issue than a matter of introducing a new set of ALPN protocol negotiation rules. This assessment is being kept as a hypothesis, without recording container type, value order, duplicate values, or the meaning of an empty collection as established requirements.

Two approaches were discussed:

- Normalize the values to a consistent shape near the TLS transport wrapper, then pass them to the subsequent paths;
- Preserve the input's compatibility boundary and let the entry point that actually uses ALPN decide whether adaptation is needed.

The former would make centralized checks easier, but would mistake transport adjacency for implementation ownership and might erase differences still visible to callers too early. The latter cannot immediately identify a single place to make the change, but would not establish a global conversion rule based on a filename alone.

The first draft chose the second approach as the decision for the investigation phase: first record collection shape as a compatibility issue visible to caller Fang Ke, without preselecting `ssltransport.py` as the sole implementation point. The follow-up needs to find an existing test or example, confirm which entry point actually observes this set of values, then use counterexamples to determine whether there is a shared place to handle them.

Three questions remain: which entry point best exposes the differences; whether existing paths depend on order, duplicate values, or an empty collection; and whether `ssltransport.py` is an actual processing point or an adjacent file encountered during the investigation. Without a concrete sample, do not expand these questions into a full specification.

# ALPN Collection Compatibility Shape Record

This record did not originally start from an already identified function. The issue first focused on the transport compatibility boundary, and an older investigation record then pointed to `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` through the issue name and call name. The direct dependencies in the file header are `from __future__ import annotations`, `io`, `socket`, and `ssl`. This explains why the investigation began near the TLS transport wrapper, but it did not make this location the conclusion. A filename can provide an entry point, but cannot by itself establish responsibility.

The complication around ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility is also here. The "collection" mentioned in the discussion does not mean that this page should specify a particular data structure; it means a group of protocol values that the negotiation path may receive, pass through, or inspect. "Shape" means whether the caller can continue to receive, compare, or pass this group of values in the original way. Unchanged protocol values do not mean that the object relationships seen by the caller remain unchanged. Conversely, a form that looks different does not automatically mean that a regression has occurred; there must still be an actual entry point showing who can see the difference.

## Earliest Assessment

The initial draft's working hypothesis was that this looked more like a representation compatibility issue than a redefinition of ALPN's negotiation capabilities. It came from the code location being examined and the issue name, not from a user path that had already been run through successfully. At that time, there was not enough material to confirm which object created the collection or whether all relevant entry points passed through the transport wrapper layer. Therefore, the initial draft did not define the container, ordering, deduplication, and empty-collection behavior as fixed rules.

This restraint had practical reasons. If a unified format is chosen first when the evidence is insufficient, and it later turns out that an entry point depends on the input's original relationships, the investigation will have difficulty distinguishing between two changes: one, the underlying negotiation is genuinely different; two, the library rewrote the shape passed to the caller at an earlier point. Once the latter happens, the original input is difficult to recover in subsequent records. Leaving the implementation point undetermined for now does not mean that any shape is acceptable; it means not making a decision yet for an entry point without samples.

## Two Directions

The first comparison was between "centralized normalization" and "adaptation at the point of use." The appeal of centralized normalization is straightforward: if all affected entry points pass through the same transport wrapper object, this location can serve as a single checkpoint, and downstream callers can more easily see a consistent form. For maintainers, one localized change is easier to read than leaving a separate exception at each of multiple entry points.

However, the material available at the time did not establish its premise. `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` was merely where the old investigation reached, and the direct dependencies only showed that it was near streams, sockets, and TLS; this information did not show that every user entry point passed through it, much less that it had permission to change the external shape of the input collection. If a path had already read the collection before reaching this location, or still needed to distinguish the original values after this location, centralized normalization might cover only half the path.
The benefit of adapting at the point of use is that it preserves differences between entry points. When a counterexample appears at a particular entry point, we can first observe what it actually receives, then decide whether conversion is needed. This avoids tying all paths to a common location that has not yet been validated. The drawback is also clear: if every finding becomes a separate exception, several entry points may adopt different interpretations of the same source, and compatibility behavior will quietly diverge.

So the second approach can only serve as an investigation sequence, not be turned directly into a permanent patchwork solution. Examining entry points one by one is meant to establish whether the differences actually exist and whether they come from the same source; it is not meant to declare in advance that each entry point has its own ALPN semantics. If multiple entry points ultimately show the same mismatch, we can then go back and compare common processing points; if the problem occurs at only one entry point, only then is there a basis for further discussion of local handling.

The initial draft made a conservative decision here: for now, do not flatten collection shapes into a single form, and do not designate `ssltransport.py` as the sole implementation point. This decision is retained, but its rationale needs to move beyond "there is not enough material yet" to verifiable limits on what has been observed.

## Where to Start Reading and Object Boundaries

For now, we still start by reading `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py`. First examine the objects actually present in the file, then follow references to find entry points where ALPN values are visible, and finally compare the caller's view before and after the change. This sequence is safer than choosing where to make changes based on the filename first, because code near transport wrapping may only handle adjacent concerns, rather than determine the collection shape.

`from __future__ import annotations` does not provide ALPN semantics. `io`, `socket`, and `ssl` also indicate only direct adjacency: the file may interact with streams, sockets, and the TLS context, but the import list does not establish where the collection is constructed, copied, or exposed. Interpreting these imports as "this is responsible for all negotiation inputs" would turn a reading clue into an implementation conclusion, a formulation the initial draft already avoided, and the revised version continues to preserve this boundary.

We also need to distinguish three observation points in time here. The first is before the value enters the negotiation path, when the caller has already handed it to an object; the second is during transport wrapping, when an object reads or forwards this set of values; the third is after negotiation has completed, when external code then sees a result or the retained input. All three may be informally referred to as "ALPN values", but the location where the collection shape changes differs, as does the compatibility impact.

If the sample only shows that TLS connection establishment succeeded, that is not enough to conclude this decision. Successful connection establishment answers whether negotiation completed; it does not answer whether the caller can still receive or compare the protocol collection in its original form. Conversely, if the form changes, we must first prove that an existing entry point can observe and depend on that change before treating it as a compatibility counterexample. What is recorded here is the object boundary, not the act of classifying all TLS environmental differences as ALPN collection issues.

## Three candidates during review

During review, the two original directions were split into three candidates to make it easier to distinguish implementation locations from investigation steps.

**Candidate A: Unify the shape near the TLS transport.**

Candidate A remains the easiest code solution to imagine. It assumes that multiple entry points share a transport-wrapper point, where normalization occurs when receiving or outputting the collection, and that downstream code handles only the agreed-upon form. It can reduce discrepancies among entry points, and it is also easy to place a local check in one location.

The problem with A is not centralization itself, but its assumptions. The current material does not show that all relevant entry points reach that point, nor that the normalization action will not change a relationship that some caller still needs to observe. If the change is made too early, downstream code will not see the original shape; if it is made too late, some entry points may already have interpreted the collection independently, and normalization may only fill in the gaps superficially. A can move from a candidate to an implementation decision only when actual samples demonstrate a common entry point and a common mismatch.

**Candidate B: Adapt independently at each use site.**

B preserves the context of each entry point. When a specific test or example exposes a difference, we can handle only the confirmed path without propagating the rule to entry points for which there is no sample. This is relatively safe given the current state of the evidence, and it makes it easier to compare exactly who saw what before and after adaptation.

The risk of B is long-term fragmentation across scattered points. If two entry points receive values from the same source but interpret the shape as different objects, callers may encounter undocumented differences when switching entry points. Therefore, B is suitable as the choice during the investigation phase, but not as an unconditional final architecture. Each local adaptation must be able to answer whether it belongs to the same category as an existing counterexample; otherwise, it merely preserves a state that has not been fully localized in more places.

**Candidate C: First establish the observable boundary, then choose the location.**

C does not first commit to the transport-wrapper layer, nor to each use site. It first requires finding an existing test or example that shows which entry point observes the collection shape; then it compares the relationships that the caller can distinguish before and after the change; if multiple entry points share the same source and the same mismatch, it then decides whether to handle them centrally. The cost of C is that it cannot immediately provide an implementation location that looks complete, but it avoids mistaking file proximity for behavioral evidence.

We are adopting C this time. A remains a candidate once a common entry point has been proven, and B remains a technique for verifying an individual path; neither becomes the final rule directly when entry-point samples are lacking. C provides not another container specification, but a selection threshold: first obtain actual observation, then discuss centralized or local handling.

## Scope of "collection shape"

To avoid later discussions misreading a working term as a complete interface contract, this section retains the content that the draft left unspecified. The collection shape here may involve whether input is still accepted, whether protocol values are passed along according to their original relationships, whether the same entry point can continue comparing these values, and whether different entry points provide incompatible external forms. The material has not yet confirmed which of these is the specific failure point.

Therefore, this page does not presuppose the following details:

- whether values have necessarily been organized before entering the transport path;
- whether input ordering has semantics that must be preserved;
- whether duplicate values have independent significance;
- whether an empty collection and no values provided must be distinguished;
- whether the negotiated result should still be viewed as the original collection;
- whether all callers share the same collection source.

These are not possibilities that have been ruled out, but implementation details that have not yet been confirmed by the material on this page. Writing them all into the decision at once would make readers think that an existing counterexample had proved each one individually. What is actually being decided now is the investigation boundary and the order for choosing a location: first confirm the entry point and the visible change, then write the necessary details into more appropriate code or regression material.

Nor can "details not presupposed" be understood in reverse as meaning that "identical content is sufficient". If a caller depends on a particular way of receiving or comparing values, then object relationships are part of the compatibility surface. Successful negotiation of the underlying protocol can only show that a transfer process was completed; it does not replace checking the collection shape. If no existing entry point can observe this difference in form, it should be recorded as an impact that has not yet been proven, rather than declaring a regression based on the formal difference.

## Revision after the counterexample was added

RHC-216 recorded `counterexample_added` in 2025-10-17. This action does not provide specific input, output, or a call stack on this page, so it cannot be expanded into a general case; what it confirms is that the previous state of "only a working hypothesis" has changed, and that at least one piece of counterevidence is worth continuing to check against existing tests or examples.

The counterexample makes an implicit judgment in the draft less tenable: as if simply not prespecifying the implementation location would prevent a compatibility risk from arising. We now withdraw this optimistic implication. Not prespecifying a location is still necessary, but it is no longer sufficient to complete the decision; the collection shape must also be treated as a checkable caller boundary, and subsequent samples must specify which entry point it appears in.

The revised judgment is neither that "existing counterexamples prove all entry points are identical", nor that "all entry points should immediately be fixed separately". It only moves the work forward one step: the phenomenon should no longer remain at the level of names and paths. The counterexample needs to be placed back into a specific entry point, so that we can observe whether it appears during input, transfer, or at a later point, and then compare the costs of A, B, C.

The local notes on the card still require using an existing test or example to trigger "ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility", and writing user paths that are not yet covered back to RHC-216. The focus of this task is to connect existing counterexamples to real entry points, not to list all theoretically possible combinations. If the existing material can replay only one path, record it as single-path evidence; you must not classify unobserved entry points as the same kind of problem, just because the issue title is broad.

2025-10-20, RHC-216 left `assignee_changed`, with the explanation that the previous person had only helped with triage, after which ownership returned to the actual maintainer. This change did not alter the technical decision, but it changed where subsequent notes should point: triage can help narrow the issue, but cannot replace a review of the collection shape and implementation location. Once responsibility is back within the actual maintainer's scope, the same card must continue to be updated with uncovered paths, rather than being treated as a finalized global conclusion.

## Current decision

The scope of ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility is defined by the compatibility boundary observable to callers, not by the path location of `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py`. For changes involving this boundary, first find an existing test or example to use as an entry point; then state whether that entry point sees the input, the collection in transit, or a later result; finally compare whether callers can continue using this set of values in the established way before and after the change.

This decision rules out two premature approaches. First, you must not claim that the file has sole responsibility for handling this based only on old investigation notes, filenames or the import relationships of `io`,`socket`,`ssl`. Second, without a specific entry point, you must not expand collection shape into a specification for ordering, deduplication, null values or a particular container.

This decision does not permanently prohibit centralized handling. If later samples show that multiple affected entry points pass through the same object, involve the same source and the same kind of shape mismatch, and that centralized handling will not erase relationships that callers still need to distinguish, then A can once again become a suitable implementation approach. If the samples cover only one entry point, B's local adaptation can still be discussed, but its scope must stay tied to that entry point, and a local counterexample must not be taken directly as proof for all entry points.

The same distinction applies to regression results. Passing test results must not merely say "negotiation succeeded", but must explain whether the collection relationships received by the caller are still usable; failing test results likewise must not merely say "different shapes", but must explain which existing entry point shows a difference as a result. Without these relationships, the results can only prompt further investigation, not automatically drive a change in implementation location.

## Historical disagreements retained after review

When the initial draft wrote "Direction 2," it was easy for readers to interpret it as having already decided that each use site would independently take on permanent compatibility work. The revision recasts it as an investigation sequence. This preserves the earlier caution without misrepresenting local handling as a long-term architecture. Reviewing each entry point one by one is intended to avoid flattening differences too early; whether to ultimately centralize is still determined by the relationships among the counterexamples.

The initial draft also described path navigation almost as an ownership determination. It now explicitly separates two things: `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` is the first reading entry point because it is close to the SSL transport wrapper; the actual handling responsibility should be determined only after the reference relationships and entry-point samples provide clarification. This adjustment does not diminish the value of that file; it simply prevents maintainers from treating the reading starting point as the only place to make changes.

Another revision is to separate "negotiation success" from "shape compatibility." The former may already be established at the lower layer, while the latter may still fail at an object boundary. If a path can complete negotiation but leaves the caller unable to receive or compare the collection as before, it should still be handled; if a form change cannot be observed by any existing entry point, the scope must not be expanded based on the form difference alone.

These changes do not rewrite past assumptions as answers that were correct in hindsight. In 2025 year 5 month, the initial draft faced path clues and unresolved questions, so it was appropriate not to lock down an implementation point yet; later counterexample records showed that entry points and decision thresholds needed to be added. What the versions actually add is the decision's executability, not a set of protocol details that the materials did not provide.

## What to Record During Review

For every additional sample added later, the content recorded on this page should center on local relationships, rather than merely saying "verified". At a minimum, it should make clear: whether the entry point came from an existing test or an example; who first observed the collection; whether the observation occurred at input, during transfer, or at the result stage; whether the caller distinguished the before-and-after change; and whether this entry point shares a source or processing point with an existing counterexample.

If a sample did not reach the expected ALPN observation point, it cannot prove collection shape compatibility; it can only show that the sample cannot answer the current question. If a sample reached the observation point but the caller behaved differently before and after the change, it is suitable for comparing centralized consolidation with local adaptation. Both cases can be traced back to RHC-216, but do not use the same phrase to obscure their differences.

If different environments produce different negotiation results, first confirm whether the difference is in the protocol result or in the object shape. Environmental changes may affect TLS negotiation conditions, but do not automatically indicate an incompatible change in the library's internal collection representation. Only when the caller-visible receiving, comparison, or transfer relationships change does it fall within the main scope of this decision.

If subsequent reading only adds code adjacency and no entry-point samples, candidate locations and reference relationships may be updated, but that alone cannot promote the transport wrapper layer to a unified handling point. If multiple user paths are added, first compare whether they observe the same source and the same kind of difference, then decide between centralization and local handling. The record should clearly state which branch this newly added material belongs to, to avoid having to infer responsibility from the filename again next time.

## Relationship to Adjacent Records

DOC-26 records HTTP/2 Proxy Tunnel Rejection, which is adjacent material from the same round of transport compatibility consolidation. It can help readers navigate to another interface review, but the conclusions about the proxy tunnel cannot be used to fill the gaps in the shape of the ALPN collection. The availability boundary of the proxy tunnel and the object boundary of the protocol collection may appear in the same transport environment, but the evidence and decisions are still stored separately.

RHC-216 appears only as a navigation entry when further counterexamples or uncovered user paths need to be investigated. The question and local action items on the card can indicate that the next step should continue checking against existing tests or examples, but they do not provide call chains, input samples, or a unified implementation conclusion that is not on this page. If later material fills in these details, specific relationships should be added rather than expanding the card title into a decision.

Likewise, `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` can remain as a source-code entry in search and reading records. Its direct dependencies are sufficient to help maintainers find the code near the TLS transport wrapper, but it is not responsible for determining all ALPN entry points on behalf of this page. To turn it into an implementation decision, specific references and user paths must provide the support, rather than the path string itself.

## Deferred Open Items

The following questions are still worth keeping, but they are not new global requirements:

- Which specific user entry does each registered counterexample fall under, and can it be replayed directly by an existing test or example;
- Whether a second entry observes the same source's ALPN collection;
- Whether there is truly a common processing point near the transport wrapper, or merely reading adjacency;
- If a common point exists, whether unified processing would erase input relationships that callers still need to distinguish;
- Among the paths subsequently added by RHC-216, which belong to the same category as the existing counterexamples and which only have similar names.

These items do not overturn the current decision. The current decision has already established the order: first confirm the compatibility boundary through the actual entry points, then choose centralized or local handling based on the evidence. The open items ask how to apply this order to the current code and samples; they do not redefine the shape of the ALPN collection.

If it ultimately turns out that no entry can distinguish a certain form difference, the checked scope and conclusion should be written back to the card instead of continuing to maintain a concern unsupported by samples. If it turns out that the differences across multiple entries are genuinely distinct, they still cannot all be unified directly; first confirm the source, invocation method, and caller usage relationship, then determine whether unification will reduce compatibility risk.

## Diagram

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    state "src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py" as ssltransport
    state "Existing tests or examples" as sample
    state "ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility" as shape
    state "RHC-216" as card
    state "Observe the boundary by calling Fang Ke" as boundary

    [*] --> ssltransport
    ssltransport --> sample
    sample --> shape
    shape --> boundary
    shape --> card
```

The starting point in the diagram is only the entry point currently retained for verification. Existing tests or examples bring the issue onto actual user paths; after the collection shapes are compared, the branches return respectively to observing the boundary by calling Fang Ke and to the RHC-216 records of counterexamples and uncovered paths. The diagram does not show the source-code entry point as the only implementation node, nor does it show the card's to-do items as conclusions already reached.

## Final decision text

This page adopts candidate C: treat ALPN Collection Shape Compatibility as a compatibility boundary observed by calling Fang Ke, first confirm the entry points using existing tests or examples, then choose a centralized or local handling point based on whether multiple entry points share the same mismatch. `src/urllib3/util/ssltransport.py` remains the starting point for reading, but is not designated in advance as the sole implementation point.

Centralized consolidation and use-site adaptation both remain candidates for later consideration. The former requires evidence of a shared entry point and evidence that caller relationships are preserved, while the latter requires limiting the scope to confirmed entry points to avoid creating unexplained scattered semantics. If new material cannot address these two conditions, retaining the current decision is more reliable than broadening the rules based on paths or names.

The next time this page is changed, what actually needs to be added is the relationship between entry points and counterexamples, or implementation trade-offs. Merely adding another way of describing a "compatible shape" will not change the decision, nor should it constitute a version change.

# HTTP/2 Proxy Tunnel Rejection Proposal

To close out this round, we're first looking separately at the path where HTTP/2 establishes a tunnel through a proxy. The earlier investigation notes point both the issue name and the call name to `src/urllib3/connection.py`, so start there to check what is visible on the connection side; the file itself is an existing Python module, with only direct imports of `annotations`, `datetime`, `logging`, and `os` at the top, which is not yet enough to establish that the proxy layer, protocol negotiation layer, and call entry point all live in the same place.

The proposal at the time was straightforward: don't let HTTP/2 connections keep using a proxy-tunneling flow that looks viable but is actually unfinished. If callers explicitly request this combination, they should receive a rejection before further connection setup begins, rather than having the incompatibility surface only after the request has been written.

There are three candidate approaches: keep the existing entry point but let it proceed further; reject the combination at the public connection entry point; or add a separate HTTP/2 tunnel implementation for proxy scenarios. The initial draft favored the second, because it would not leave users guessing about a half-finished path. The trade-off is that existing callers would fail earlier, and we need to confirm whether the rejection point covers all proxy configurations.

Still unconfirmed: whether rejection should happen when the tunnel is configured or when the connection is actually created; ordinary HTTP/1.1 tunnels must not be blocked as a side effect of this change; the order in which proxy authentication headers and TLS configuration are prepared has not been checked either. In the next round, first trace back from existing callers to verify the entry point, then decide whether to turn this proposal into an implementation change.

# HTTP/2 Proxy Tunnel Rejection Proposal

The initial draft assumed that "adding a rejection branch to the connection object" would be enough. After review, that statement remains, but it is no longer treated as a settled conclusion about where to implement the change. The old records do link the issue name and the call name to `src/urllib3/connection.py`; that file is a useful starting point for follow-up investigation, but the few direct imports at the top of the file do not establish that it must own all the proxy logic.

This discussion starts by separating two scenarios that are easy to conflate. In one, the caller has already selected a proxy and requested a tunnel; in the other, the connection is later prepared using HTTP/2. The former describes intent; the latter describes a protocol path. Reporting an error only at a later point still looks like a "rejection," but can lead callers to mistake proxy configuration, authentication setup, or a connection failure for the cause. Rejecting earlier changes the timing of existing retries and exception handling.

The recommendation therefore remains: treat the combination of HTTP/2 and proxy tunneling as unsupported, and reject it at a point where that combination is identifiable but no irreversible network action has started. "Earlier" here does not mean that all proxy requests must be intercepted at the same layer. Ordinary proxy requests and non-HTTP/2 connections should continue to use their existing entry points; this proposal is limited to cases where a tunnel is requested and the target path is HTTP/2.

### Counterexamples Raised During Review

- Checking only whether proxy configuration exists is not enough. A proxy may be used for ordinary requests; that does not mean the caller requested a tunnel.
- Checking only the connection object's final type is not enough either. If tunnel setup has already happened, a later rejection leaves behind some already-executed setup actions.
- Treating all exceptions as TLS issues would obscure the caller's choice. Proxy authentication, certificate configuration, and protocol negotiation may all be involved at once, but they are not the same condition to check.
- Silently falling back to HTTP/1.1 so existing callers can "keep working" is outside this proposal's scope. That would replace the caller's chosen transport semantics with an implicit fallback, and the downgrade would not be apparent during debugging.

During review, someone proposed adding a complete HTTP/2 proxy tunnel implementation outright, then using capability detection to decide whether to use it. That direction was not ruled out, but it is not a small fix: it requires specifying who owns connection state after the tunnel is established, at what stage authentication headers are introduced, and whether the connection can still be returned to the pool on failure. The available material does not answer these questions, so this cannot be presented as an option with the same cost as an early rejection branch.

### Tentative Decision

This page still favors explicit rejection over silent fallback, and does not commit to a new tunnel implementation in this round. The implementation should be able to distinguish between "a proxy is present" and "a tunnel is being requested." If the caller has not requested a tunnel, this proposal should not change their path.

The original statement, "reject uniformly at the public entry point," is now marked as too broad. Whether the public entry point can see the complete set of conditions has not yet been confirmed; if the full condition can only be assembled later in connection preparation, the choice should be based on the state actually visible at that point. The rejection point needs to meet both requirements: the error should come no later than network activity, and ordinary proxy connections must not be incorrectly blocked just to report the error sooner.

### Withdrawal Conditions

If follow-up investigation shows that a HTTP/2 proxy tunnel implementation already exists, and callers can get stable behavior for connection handling, authentication, and failure cleanup, this rejection proposal should be withdrawn and replaced with a record of the support boundaries. If it turns out that the entry point cannot identify tunnel intent before writing out the request, the "early rejection" wording should also be withdrawn; first fill in the missing state propagation, then compare locations again.

At present, `src/urllib3/connection.py` remains the only local starting point that can be reliably rechecked. For the failed run on the release side, see DOC-27; it can help guide follow-up questions about whether the same kind of combination surfaced during release, but it cannot replace the assessment of the connection path here.

# HTTP/2 Proxy Tunnel Rejection Proposal

This proposal is still cited because it preserves several inconsistent assessments made during closeout. The earliest version treated "HTTP/2 Proxy Tunnel Rejection" as a small change in the connection layer; a later review found that the first question was where caller intent, proxy state, and the protocol path are all visible at the same time, and only then which method should throw the exception. The early recommendations in the document have not been removed, to help explain why the later work did not proceed with the idea of "a blanket approach at the public entry point".

The current follow-up review starts at `src/urllib3/connection.py`. The old investigation notes led to this path through the issue name and the call name; in the revision at the time, `from __future__ import annotations`, `import datetime`, `import logging`, and `import os` were visible at the top of the file. These details only indicate that this is a starting point for reading the connection-side code, and cannot replace a review of the actual call path. The verification request recorded in RHC-217 is also very narrow: find callers that still use this rejection behavior, and check their actual versions, entry points, and current results.

## Retained Initial-Draft Assessments

The initial draft argued that once a caller requests a tunnel through a proxy, and the target connection is being prepared to use HTTP/2, it should receive an explicit rejection rather than continue attempting a combination for which support has not been promised. This overall direction was not overturned. It avoids a worse experience: after the caller hands its configuration to the transport layer, connection preparation begins and some state has already changed, only to end in a failure tangled up with the proxy, authentication, or TLS.

The initial draft also said "reject at the public connection entry point". This sentence was later crossed out, but the original wording was retained. It treated "all conditions are already visible at the entry point" as an established fact, which the review did not confirm. Whether a proxy object exists, whether the request needs a tunnel, and whether the connection will be handled using HTTP/2 may become available at different stages. A shared branch placed too early would block ordinary proxy requests; one placed too late would make the rejection meaningless.

The three candidate approaches listed at the time are below, still in the order of the original discussion:

1. Add no further checks, and continue with the existing connection preparation. This is the lowest-cost approach, but it would make an unsupported combination surface as some other kind of failure, leaving callers unable to tell whether to change their proxy settings or protocol selection.
2. Explicitly reject recognized HTTP/2 tunnel requests. This makes the boundary visible to the caller Fang Ke, but requires choosing the right detection point and verifying that non-tunnel routing remains unchanged.
3. Add an implementation of HTTP/2 proxy tunnels. This might improve capability coverage, but it is more than adding a branch; connection return, proxy authentication, TLS preparation, failure cleanup, and retry behavior would all need to be specified again.

The initial preference was for the second option, not because it would always be better than the third, but because no material at the time showed that the third option's lifecycle was ready to ship. This assessment was a conservative choice for closeout, not a rejection of a future implementation.

## Distinctions Added After a Review

The review separated "proxy" into two different questions. A proxy appearing in the configuration does not automatically mean that the caller will establish a tunnel; an ordinary proxy request should not be rejected simply because the protocol name contains HTTP/2. Conversely, when the caller explicitly specifies tunnel intent, it is not acceptable to wait until the request has already been written and then explain after the fact that it is unsupported. The proposal therefore requires all of these conditions to hold: a proxy path exists, the caller requests a tunnel, and the target connection uses HTTP/2. If any condition is missing, the combination is outside the scope of this page.

An edge case that was not handled well at the time is also retained here. Proxy authentication headers may be prepared before the connection is established, and the TLS context may already have been configured for the target connection. Early versions treated all of this preparation as "harmless preliminary steps", which was overly optimistic. Even without network writes, state constructed in advance can affect failure logs and the caller's assessment; however, the existing records do not provide sufficient grounds to specify the step at which these preparations must occur. This page therefore does not treat authentication headers or TLS configuration as rejection conditions, and only requires the follow-up review to confirm that they have not been mistaken for the root cause.

Another approach discussed was silently falling back to HTTP/1.1. This appears to reduce failures, but it turns the caller's selected protocol into an implicit policy: when a request succeeds, the caller does not know that a different transport path was used, and when it fails, the caller cannot tell whether the proxy lacks the required capability or the fallback behaves differently. This approach was not included in the list of recommendations. If fallback for compatibility is genuinely needed in the future, it should have its own proposal stating the selection conditions and what the caller can see; it must not be tucked into the rejection branch.

## Earlier Disagreements About Placement

"Reject when configuring the tunnel" was once the most intuitive formulation. Its advantage is that the caller gets a result as soon as it expresses its intent, and subsequent connection preparation does not need to continue. The question is whether the tunnel configuration step can already reliably determine that HTTP/2 will ultimately be used, and the old records did not give a definite answer.

"Reject when creating the connection" defers evaluating the conditions until the protocol path is clearer. It reduces misclassification, but carries a risk: if tunnel-related state has already been consumed or request preparation has advanced, the caller will see the later failure as a connection error rather than an unsupported combination. The initial draft did not distinguish these two costs, and only said "report the error as early as possible", which was corrected later.

The selection principle retained now is not a fixed method name, but two constraints: when rejection occurs, it must already be possible to distinguish tunnel intent from ordinary proxying; no irreversible network action may begin before rejection. If both conditions cannot be met at the same point, do not hide a gap in state propagation behind a seemingly tidy branch. First add the connection state needed to make the conditions visible, then reconsider the rejection point.

This principle also explains why the location of the `connection.py` path alone cannot determine where the implementation belongs. That path was the earliest navigation point, not evidence that all checks should be in the file. During follow-up review, trace the actual caller to establish: where it configures the proxy, when it expresses tunnel intent, when it selects HTTP/2, and whether it can still abort before entering connection preparation. RHC-217 can be used to record the specific adopters and versions found in this follow-up review.

## Patch-Style Approaches That Were Not Adopted

Someone suggested rewriting the exception text only when the connection ultimately fails, to let users know that proxy tunnels are unsupported. This suggestion was not adopted. By the point of failure, proxy authentication, TLS validation, or connection-pool state may already be mixed in, and rewriting the text would disguise a diagnostic clue as a precise statement of capability. Nor would it prevent callers from placing their retry strategy at the wrong point.

Someone also suggested always turning off HTTP/2 whenever a proxy configuration is detected. This proposal was not adopted either. It broadens "a proxy exists" into "a proxy necessarily requires a tunnel", and would deprive proxy requests that do not need a tunnel of their original choices. The early version did not explicitly state this counterexample, making "reject at the public entry point" easy to interpret as blanket disabling; with this addition here, the old wording is still retained above.

The final approach was to let the call proceed, wait for the proxy to produce a result, and then leave the caller to identify it on its own. This might be sufficient during experimentation, but not for closeout. The result the caller receives will vary with proxy, network, and authentication state, making a stable boundary difficult to establish. The value of explicit rejection is not that it reduces all errors, but that it makes the failure mode of this known unsupported combination independent of the external environment.

## What to Check If Rejection Is Retained

If a later implementation still follows this proposal, first confirm whether the caller really requests a tunnel. Seeing only a proxy address or proxy object should not trigger rejection. Then confirm that the connection will be handled using HTTP/2; if protocol selection has not yet been determined, it must not be aborted based on a guess. Finally, check that rejection happens before the request is written, and check that ordinary HTTP/1.1 tunnels and proxy requests that do not need a tunnel remain unchanged.

This does not require revalidating all proxy behavior. The focus is on three adjacent scenarios: ordinary proxying without configuring a tunnel; configuring a tunnel without using HTTP/2; and satisfying both conditions. The first two guard against overly broad conditions, while the third confirms that the rejection is not swallowed by the subsequent connection flow. If the actual caller has authentication or TLS configuration, record the stages at which they appear, rather than attributing them to this rejection logic just because they coexist in the same run.

The recommendation is to keep the failure result as a clear "unsupported" signal, rather than a generic connection failure. The specific exception type and text must be determined by the implementation and the current state of callers; that part was never finalized on this page. The early draft emphasized only "explicit", without providing an error message format that could be copied directly, so this old proposal should not be used as the basis for interface wording.

## Withdrawal and Migration

If follow-up review finds that usable HTTP/2 proxy tunnel support already exists, with consistent behavior for connection creation, authentication preparation, failure cleanup, and connection return, then the rejection recommendation on this page should be withdrawn. Withdrawal does not mean deleting the old records: it must explain which callers migrate from rejection to the supported path, and whether the old error handling still catches exceptions too broadly.

If it turns out that the protocol and tunnel intent cannot both be known before network actions, the promise of "immediate rejection" should also be withdrawn. In that case, addressing state propagation between adjacent layers comes before inserting a check at some entry point. The original closeout goal was to keep unsupported combinations from masquerading as incidental failures; if the conditions themselves are not yet visible, forcing an early failure would only create another kind of misclassification.

Adding a complete tunnel implementation remains an open option, but it requires a separate design document. At a minimum, that document must answer who owns the connection, how cleanup works after failure, where proxy authentication enters the flow, and how callers distinguish the supported path from the old rejection path. Folding those questions into this page would misrepresent an old proposal about the rejection boundary as an implementation design.

## Items Still Requiring Follow-Up Review

- The existing adopters referenced by RHC-217: their actual versions, entry points into the connection side, and the results currently observed.
- The area around `src/urllib3/connection.py`: the stages at which tunnel intent and HTTP/2 selection become available, respectively.
- Ordinary HTTP/1.1 tunnels: whether they pass through the same check point.
- Proxy authentication and TLS preparation: whether they have already left state before rejection that could mislead the investigation.

DOC-27 record a failed run of release automation. This can provide a timing clue when similar symptoms appear during a release, but is not evidence that the core connection path already supports or rejects a particular combination. The old conclusions on this page should be rechecked only against the call entry points and connection state described above.

# Release Cache vs. Original Live State Trade-off

This page is still used to look up "why wasn't it rebuilt at the time?" Start with the retained artifacts; don't treat this as the current release process: what is preserved here is a trade-off between the cache and the original live state. Callers were later disabled, rollback checks were performed, and new design comparisons were made after this decision.

The initial debate was straightforward. One side wanted to rebuild the release environment and reproduce the request target once; the other argued for freezing the current revision first, because the failure path was already tied to the live state. At the time, what was available was the hit entry and some of the before-and-after state; what wasn't available was the full command arguments and callers confirmed to be part of regression testing. If the environment were switched first, the cache hit, remnants of old tasks, and new build queue would all change at once, and the result would no longer tell us about the original live state.

The TLS context was also listed at the time as a possible split point. That wording remains in the old draft, but it should not be read as a technical choice that had already been made. It was only a direction for comparison: the request target and the TLS context might take different failure paths, so one rebuild could not answer both questions. The original record does not contain enough material to show which active caller should take over regression after a split, and the full command was not recovered; neither gap can be closed by one successful rerun.

## What Was Decided at the Time

The decision was to pin the current entry, export the state before and after the failure, and then allow the environment to exit; the environment would not be rebuilt to fill out the old record. New results produced after exit are recorded separately and cannot be compared side by side with the original run. The recovery action also restores only the old entry; it does not replace the old live state with a cleaned-up green state. This decision addresses how the record is preserved, not whether cache behavior has been explained.

The corresponding artifact entry is still `docs/adj-urllib3/decisions/urllib3-release-automation-cache-vs-original-state-tradeoff.md`. It is not especially tidy: early notes described the "current revision" as a sufficient basis for reproduction, but in reality it is only an anchor for locating the original scenario, not a complete environment definition. The missing full command has not been filled in, so the old wording remains misleading, but it has not been removed.

The RHCA-013 item was later canceled because the required information was moved to and maintained through an existing registry entry. This made the case for rebuilding an environment for the old ticket weaker, but did not prove that the cache itself was irrelevant. The RHCA-016 item was also later canceled because the caller had stopped using that path, so no fix was scheduled; the parameter gap it left remains, but it is no longer worth recovering in the name of a fix. The cancellation reasons for the two cards differ: the former moved the information to an existing entry, while the latter reflects that the caller no longer uses the original path. They cannot be collapsed into "the issue is resolved."

## Later Exit Actions

The RHCA-019 item had design comparisons recorded before and after the environment changed, and work on it resumed later; this shows that the original retention action only solved "don't lose the live state" and did not replace a new design decision. The RHCA-022 item completed rollback checks, but after the window ended, the current entry may still come from the old cache or old task; this question is not resolved on this page. The existence of rollback checks also cannot be taken to mean that the cache source at the time had been distinguished.

Accordingly, the old draft's claim that "pinning the entry is enough to determine the cache" should be marked as no longer applicable. An entry may continue to exist without still pointing to the original queue, and that does not mean a state observed later still belongs to the original live state. Rollback checks can only show that the rollback action was checked; they cannot fill in the command arguments, much less distinguish old tasks from the cache source. The later design comparison likewise cannot be projected backward into a choice that had already been made early on.

The decision retained here is narrow:

- For an existing live state, retain the hit entry and the state before and after the failure, avoiding changes to both the environment and the object being evaluated in the same run.
- For paths that have already been retired or whose callers have stopped using them, do not start a rebuild intended to reproduce the old issue.
- For the split proposal involving the TLS context, retain it as a proposal that was not adopted at the time; it does not automatically become the default route for later design.

If someone only needs to find the artifacts from that time, follow the decision document above. If the goal is to determine where the entry after the window ended came from, start again with the rollback checks in RHCA-022 and the design comparison in RHCA-019, rather than applying this page's old conclusion directly. The DOC-31 item records questions left by the users and cannot be used to fill in the missing command or environment details.

This record is retained to this day because "not rebuilding" itself still explains why the old materials are incomplete—not because it gives the correct approach to current release automation.

# Documentation Site Old-to-New Entry Point Migration Index

The documentation site's entry points aren't limited to a single directory link. Explanatory pages in docs, links from guide, references in release notes, and old links still in use all take users to different places. Handle each entry point individually during migration; don't merge records just because the pages have the same name.

The index file remains at `docs/adj-dummyserver/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Each row must retain at least four things: where the old entry point is referenced, where its replacement is, which callers still go through the old entry point, and which source revision the record is based on. If no consumer has been traced, mark the status as pending confirmation; it must not be changed to migrated.

```text
Before migration
  Old navigation ────────> Old page
  Release notes ──────> Old page
  Consumers ────────> Old page

During migration
  Old navigation ────────> Current entry point
  Release notes ──────> Current entry point
  Consumers ────────> Old page or current entry point

After completion
  Historical records ──────> Retain old entry point and date
  Visible navigation ──────> Current entry point
```

## Create the index rows first

Start with the entry points currently visible on the documentation site, rather than guessing at old pages from directory names. Add a record for each entry point:

- Old entry point: retain the original text and the documentation page it appears on; don't erase the record even if the old entry point is no longer accessible.
- Replacement location: record the relative location of the current entry point, along with the docs or guide area it is in.
- Consumers: record only people or pages that can actually still reach the documentation site through the old entry point; mark as pending confirmation if unclear.
- Release notes: record the release notes that need to be updated at the same time, so they don't keep sending people back to the old page after the new navigation has switched over.
- Disposition: distinguish between three actions: "change to a redirect," "keep as history," and "await confirmation."

Index rows are not a release checklist. Their purpose is to show why an old entry point was kept when the next cleanup happens, not to collect every page's content in one place.

## Migration batches

Each batch handles only a group of entry points that can be confirmed together. For example, if a guide already has a replacement location but the release notes haven't been updated, first point the guide's visible navigation to the current entry point; leave the release notes for the next batch. Don't declare an old entry point invalid early just to keep the batches tidy.

Before starting a batch, copy the old entry point's original location and source revision. Then handle the replacement location before changing the visible navigation. After making the changes, read the current revision through the regular-account entry point. If the page isn't visible or access is denied, retain the location where access was denied in the index; you must not use the admin view to mark this item as visible. Whether a page is visible through the documentation site's regular entry point and whether a maintainer can find the file internally are two different things.

During migration, caller Fang Ke may temporarily continue using the old entry point, but the index must show which batch it belongs to. This keeps later cleanup from mistaking an entry point "being migrated" for an "unused remnant."

## Handling old documentation

There are two types of old documentation. One is just outdated navigation and can be removed from visible menus after being updated to point to the current entry point; the other preserves version context and should remain available for reference. The latter must not be rewritten as current documentation or reduced to a redirect with no context. When keeping it, retain at least the old entry point's text, the original record date, and the replacement location.

If the old documentation describes an obsolete procedure, the page can be marked as applying only to the old entry point; don't mix it into the current guide. Keep only current entry points and procedures that are still valid in the current guide. The value of the old page is in explaining why some consumers still arrive with old links.

## Rollback

If the replacement entry point has an error, regular accounts can't read the current revision, or a registered caller can't complete the redirect, first restore the old entry points for that batch. Rollback does not mean deleting the current entry point: keep both the current entry point and the records already updated, mark the batch as rolled back in the index, and record the entry point that triggered the rollback.

After restoring access, check the path taken by the original consumer again. If the old entry point is readable but the current one is not, first stop any further cleanup of navigation in the same batch. If both are readable but the release notes still point to the old page, handle only the release notes; don't roll back the whole batch.

## Stop maintaining old entry points

Stop maintaining an old entry point only once its replacement is visible, registered callers no longer depend on the old entry point, and historical records still allow the old page's source to be traced. Stopping maintenance doesn't mean deleting history; keep this migration record in the index for later reorganization of the documentation site.

Who will maintain this long term hasn't been decided here. When taking over, first check the callers marked pending confirmation and the rolled-back batches in the index, then handle new cases of outdated navigation.
